newsitem.title: UK: British unemployment falls to six year low.
newsitem.headline: British unemployment falls to six year low.

text.p: British unemployment fell 67,800 in January to the lowest rate for six years, official figures showed on Wednesday, giving the government a welcome boost before the general election.
The Office for National Statistics said 1.815 million, or 6.5 percent of the working population, were unemployed and seeking benefit compared with 1.883 million in December.
But the official figures also showed earnings growth accelerated at the end of last year, raising the prospect of higher inflation in the future.
Underlying average earnings grew 4.25 percent in December, and November growth was revised up to 4.25 percent from an original estimate of 4.0 percent.

The government welcomed the fall in unemployment and played down worries that higher wages signalled higher prices down the line. "Performance-related bonuses and overtime largely account for a small rise in average earnings growth," a Treasury official said. "There is no sign of any pickup in wage settlements."

However City economists, who had forecast a smaller 30,000 monthly drop, said the higher earnings figures were bad news for the government, and Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke in particular. He is charged with hitting a tough 2.5 percent inflation target.
"The worst news for the government and (financial) markets is the acceleration in underlying average earnings," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at Bank America.
The figures would probably not lead to higher interest rates before the election, which must be held by May, but would increase pressure for a rise soon after.

"The labour market data are strong and, while unlikely to prompt a near-term tightening of policy, they will increase speculation that rates will have to be hiked immediately after the election," said Hawkins.
Earlier on Wednesday, Clarke dismissed calls by the Bank of England for higher interest rates.
He told a radio interviewer that the strong pound was having a big deflationary effect on the British economy and said he saw no need for tighter credit.

But he sought to play down the extent of any disagreement between the government and the Bank. "I am disagreeing with him (Bank of England Governor Eddie Goerge) over one quarter of one percent on interest rates," Clarke said.
Interest rates were last raised on October 30 last year, by a quarter point to 6.0 percent.
